title_en: Letter to Xystus, Bishop of Rome
author: Cyril of Alexandria
occasion: The fragment does not specify the occasion; Cyril makes a declarative statement about his own beliefs without context of accusation or defense.
argument: Cyril denies ever holding any view contrary to the truth or ever calling the divine nature of the Word passible. He affirms that the nature of God is impassible, unchangeable, and invariable, even in the nature of humanity. He confesses one Christ in both natures and from both natures.

outline.move: Cyril denies teaching that the divine nature of the Word is passible and confesses God's impassible, unchangeable nature and one Christ in and from both natures.

cast.name: Cyril
cast.who: Bishop of Alexandria and author of the letter.

cast.name: Xystus
cast.who: Bishop of Rome to whom the letter is addressed.

key_terms.sense: Passible, capable of suffering, applied to the divine nature of the Word.
Impassible, incapable of suffering, a property of the divine nature.
Unchangeable, not subject to change, a property of the divine nature.
Invariable, not subject to alteration, a property of the divine nature.
Nature, the essential character of a thing, used of both the divine nature of the Word and the nature of humanity.
The Word, the divine Son of God, whose nature Cyril denies is passible.
Christ, the one subject who is in and from both the divine and human natures.

scripture: No scripture is cited in this fragment.
uncertain: The exact date of the letter is not stated in the source.
The full original context of the letter is not preserved; only a fragment is given.
The source heading contains a textual correction: Ἰούστον is corrected to Ξύστον, indicating some manuscript uncertainty about the addressee's name.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He affirms that the nature of God is impassible, unchangeable, and invariable, even in the nature of humanity.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οἶδα δὲ καὶ ἀπαθῆ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ φύσιν καὶ ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον, κὰν τῇ τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος φύσει
_unresolved_facts.fix: He affirms that the nature of God is impassible, unchangeable, and invariable, even in the nature of humanity (κἂν τῇ τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος φύσει = 'even in the nature of humanity' or 'although in the nature of humanity').

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Κυρίλλου ἐκ τῆς πρὸς Ἰούστον [ξορρ. Ξύστον] ἐπίσκοπον Ῥώμης ἐπιστολῆς
_unresolved_facts.fix: Xystus, source_forms: ["Ξύστον"], with note that the manuscript reads Ἰούστον corrected to Ξύστον
